name: Tinefold Design
statement: Build an AI-driven brainstorming tool for IT and software problems. The user states a problem; the AI proposes solution options; each chosen solution breaks into sub-problems, which the AI expands again. The result is an AND-OR graph: problems where one solution is picked, solutions where every sub-problem must be solved. The AI expands nodes; the user controls every selection.

steps.reason: Audience, scale and model access decide storage and hosting before any option makes sense.

items.title: Who is it for, how many people collaborate, and on what surface?
items.summary: Audience, collaboration and surface change every option below.
options: Solo: one user per graph, web app with a canvas

answer.option: Solo: one user per graph, web app with a canvas
answer.freeText: A learning project first: brainstorm my own software problems and learn the AI mechanics by building them. Later open source, with pluggable models and task types (classify, describe, plan).

items.title: How large do graphs get?
items.summary: Decides whether a call can see the whole graph or must filter it.

answer.freeText: I do not know yet. Assume hundreds, not thousands; if that is wrong, context compilation needs filtering earlier.

items.title: Which models will it call?
items.summary: Local models change hosting and CORS; API keys alone keep the browser path simple.
options: Anthropic or OpenAI with my own API keys

answer.option: Anthropic or OpenAI with my own API keys

items.title: Server-backed web app (Node + Postgres)
items.summary: A conventional web app: Node API, Postgres for graphs and events, React front end. Keys and provider calls stay on the server.
cons: A backend to host and operate for a one-person tool
Every provider call hops through the server
Slower to get the first expansion working

items.title: Engine library + thin host
items.summary: Put every rule in a pure TypeScript engine and wrap it in the thinnest host that works, so the host can change later without touching the rules.
pros: Rules are testable without a UI
The host can be swapped later
cons: Still needs a host decision before anything runs

items.title: Local-first desktop app
items.summary: An Electron or Tauri shell with local files, calling providers from the desktop.
cons: Packaging and updates for one user

steps.recommended: Engine library + thin host
steps.reason: A pure engine keeps the rules testable and lets the host change once the hosting question is really settled.
assumptions: Hundreds of nodes per graph, not thousands
Anthropic and OpenAI both enforce output schemas
A backend is allowed but not required
steps.choose: Server-backed web app (Node + Postgres)

items.title: Storage model
items.summary: How a graph, its immutable node versions and its history are persisted.

items.title: Expansion contract
items.summary: The JSON every expansion must return, and how to make models honour it.

items.title: Context compilation
items.summary: What each LLM call sees, and how to keep it deterministic and within budget.

items.title: Staleness tracking
items.summary: How a change upstream marks dependent decisions, and when to re-check them.

items.title: Graph canvas UI
items.summary: How the AND-OR graph, selections and stale marks are shown and acted on.

items.title: PRD generation
items.summary: How the decided subtree becomes a document.

items.title: Relational tables
items.summary: Nodes, versions, edges and selections as normalised tables; history through audit columns.

items.title: Document per graph + append-only event log
items.summary: Each graph is one document (the snapshot) plus an ordered log of events; the document is only a cache of folding the log. Where it lives follows the host.
pros: History, export and earlier versions come free
One user, so loading the whole graph is fine
Derive everything on read, in memory
cons: Snapshot and log can drift without discipline

items.title: Pure event-sourced with replay
items.summary: Only the log is stored; every open replays it from the start.

steps.recommended: Document per graph + append-only event log
steps.reason: One user and whole-graph loads make a snapshot plus log the cheapest model that still keeps history.
steps.choose: Document per graph + append-only event log

items.title: Provider-enforced schema
items.summary: Use the provider's native structured output (tool use or JSON schema) so the shape is guaranteed by the API.
cons: A schema guarantees shape, not sense

items.title: Model-agnostic prompted JSON only
items.summary: Ask for JSON in the prompt, validate with a schema, retry with the error appended on failure.

items.title: Two-phase reason-then-extract
items.summary: A free-text reasoning call first, then a second call that extracts the JSON.

steps.recommended: Provider-enforced schema
steps.reason: Both target providers enforce schemas today; validation on top catches what the schema cannot.
assumptions: Anthropic and OpenAI both enforce output schemas
steps.choose: Provider-enforced schema

steps.axis: how much of the graph each call sees

items.title: Full context with a hard ceiling, condensed past the soft ceiling
items.summary: Every call gets the root, comments, a code-rendered decision summary of the active subtree and this node's ancestor chain. Tokens are logged per call. Past a soft ceiling the summary is swapped for a model condensation cached on its hash; past a hard ceiling the call is refused.
pros: Deterministic: same state in, same bytes out
The token log says when filtering becomes necessary, with numbers

items.title: Relevance-filtered via embeddings
items.summary: Embed nodes and include only the most relevant ones per call.
cons: An embedding pipeline before any value

steps.recommended: Full context with a hard ceiling, condensed past the soft ceiling
steps.reason: The decision summary is rendered by code, never by a model, so it cannot drift; filtering can wait for the numbers.
steps.choose: Full context with a hard ceiling, condensed past the soft ceiling

steps.text: Storage is a document per graph plus an event log, so no backend is needed at all: the browser can hold it and call the providers directly with my own keys. Also use more than one provider, chosen per stage (expansion, classification, stale check), with one default.

steps.reason: The comment removes the need for a server: with a document plus event log the browser can store everything and call providers itself, which contradicts this choice.

steps.statement: Build an AI-driven brainstorming tool for IT and software problems. The user states a problem; the AI proposes solution options; each chosen solution breaks into sub-problems, which the AI expands again. The result is an AND-OR graph: problems where one solution is picked, solutions where every sub-problem must be solved. The AI expands nodes; the user controls every selection. No backend is required: the app runs in the browser, stores each graph as a document plus an event log, and calls LLM providers directly with the user's own API keys. A default provider applies, with per-stage overrides (expansion, classification, stale check). Later the tool is open source, so others can attach their own models and task types (classify, describe, plan).

items.title: Browser-only SPA
items.summary: A static site: React app, IndexedDB for graphs, direct provider calls from the browser with the user's keys. No server of any kind.
cons: Local models need CORS or a shell

items.title: Browser + optional thin server
items.summary: The same SPA plus an optional small server for sync and as a provider proxy.
pros: Keeps a door open for sharing
cons: An abstraction for a server that may never exist

items.title: Desktop shell (Tauri/Electron)
items.summary: The same app inside a desktop shell with local files and no CORS limits.
cons: Not a link you can open anywhere

steps.recommended: Browser-only SPA
steps.reason: Matches the rewritten problem without an abstraction for a server that may never exist. Revisit a desktop shell before building a proxy if local models become real.
assumptions: No backend is a soft constraint: not required, optional later
API keys only for the MVP; local models (Ollama, LM Studio) later
One default provider with per-stage overrides
steps.choose: Browser-only SPA

items.title: Code structure: engine and client
items.summary: Where the graph rules live and how the UI relates to them.

items.title: Expansion contract
items.summary: Re-decided for the browser: the JSON every expansion returns and how models honour it across providers.

items.title: Provider registry and key storage
items.summary: Adapter interface, per-stage model mapping, where keys live in the browser, per-provider browser-call quirks.

items.title: Staleness tracking
items.summary: Dependency recording per node, red and yellow marks, the cheap on-open check, the restart-from-here warning.

items.title: Graph canvas UI
items.summary: Layout, chosen-subtree highlight, disabled dimming, stale marks, comment entry, assumption display.

items.title: Output documents
items.summary: How decisions become the document the user actually needs, and how it is cached.

items.title: Separate engine package + thin web client
items.summary: A pure TypeScript engine (event log, reducer, selectors, context compiler, providers, documents) with no DOM, published as a package; a React client that only renders engine state and forwards clicks. One spec and one CLAUDE.md per side.
pros: Every rule testable without a UI, under a mock provider
The client can be replaced (CLI, desktop) without touching rules
Clear handover: engine milestones before client milestones
cons: Two packages to version and link
A feature the client needs must land in the engine first

items.title: One React app with graph logic inside
items.summary: Keep the reducer and selectors next to the components.
cons: Hard to test without the DOM

steps.recommended: Separate engine package + thin web client
steps.reason: The engine owns every rule in the PRD; the client is a rendering system over it. The client never computes a graph fact.
steps.choose: Separate engine package + thin web client

steps.node: Separate engine package + thin web client

items.title: Clarifying questions policy
items.summary: When the model may ask instead of expand, and how often.

items.title: Regeneration semantics
items.summary: What 'regenerate' rewrites and what it keeps.

items.title: Publishing the engine to npm
items.summary: Versioning, the package boundary, and how the client pins it. Today the client links the sibling folder.

items.title: Sharing a sub-problem across branches
items.summary: The same sub-problem under two solutions: the identity rule (problem text plus inherited constraints) and whether decisions merge automatically. Ported copies by hand for now.

steps.axis: how often the model may ask

items.title: One clarify round per node, up to three questions with answer choices, skippable
items.summary: The first expansion of a node may ask up to three questions, each with two to five answer options plus free text. The next expansion is shown the answers and may not ask again. The user can continue without answering.
pros: Missing facts get asked once, at the right node
Answers feed the context and staleness
cons: A second round of questions needs a regenerate

items.title: Ask freely, as many rounds as the model wants
items.summary: Every expansion may ask again.

items.title: Never ask; assume and list the assumptions
items.summary: The model always expands and records what it assumed instead.

steps.recommended: One clarify round per node, up to three questions with answer choices, skippable
steps.reason: Asking once, where the fact matters, is the middle ground; assumptions are still recorded for everything not asked.
steps.choose: One clarify round per node, up to three questions with answer choices, skippable

items.title: Regenerate the node only, as a new immutable version
items.summary: A new version of one node for the current context, with no children. The client chains regenerate then expand when the user regenerates an expanded problem. Old versions and their subtrees stay stored, disabled.
cons: Sub-problems under the old version go dim and must be re-expanded

items.title: Regenerate the whole subtree
items.summary: One click rewrites the node and everything beneath it.

steps.recommended: Regenerate the node only, as a new immutable version
steps.reason: Immutable versions are the rule everywhere else; the subtree variant would break it.
steps.choose: Regenerate the node only, as a new immutable version

steps.axis: how structure is enforced across providers

items.title: Adapter per provider: native structured output where available, prompted JSON + schema validation as fallback
items.summary: Anthropic uses forced tool use; any OpenAI-compatible endpoint gets the prompted-schema path. Every output is validated with Zod regardless, and retried once with the error appended.
pros: The adapter boundary is needed for the provider registry anyway
Validate even enforced output: a schema guarantees shape, not sense
Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works, including local servers

items.title: Model-agnostic prompted JSON only
items.summary: Ask for JSON in the prompt and validate; no native structured output anywhere.
cons: Gives up a guarantee the main providers offer

items.title: Two-phase reason-then-extract
items.summary: A reasoning call, then an extraction call.

steps.recommended: Adapter per provider: native structured output where available, prompted JSON + schema validation as fallback
steps.reason: Re-decided after the rewrite: the browser talks to several providers directly, so an adapter per provider is unavoidable.
steps.choose: Adapter per provider: native structured output where available, prompted JSON + schema validation as fallback

steps.axis: how models are chosen and keys kept

items.title: Registry with one default model and per-stage overrides; keys in localStorage; direct browser calls
items.summary: Stages: expand, stale check, summarize, document. Settings hold a default provider and model plus optional overrides per stage. Keys stay in localStorage and are sent only to their provider. With no key, a demo mode answers from a mock provider.
pros: A cheap model for stale checks, a strong one for expansions
No key leaves the browser except to its own provider
Works with no key at all
cons: localStorage is readable by any script on the origin
Manual per-stage configuration is a burden if overused

items.title: A single model for everything
items.summary: One provider, one model, no stages.
cons: Loses the cost lever for cheap checks

items.title: Keys held by a proxy server
items.summary: The browser calls a proxy that holds the keys.
cons: Needs the server that was just rejected

steps.recommended: Registry with one default model and per-stage overrides; keys in localStorage; direct browser calls
steps.reason: Per-stage overrides keep the cost lever without forcing configuration; the default covers everyone else.
assumptions: Anthropic and OpenAI both allow direct browser calls with the right header
steps.choose: Registry with one default model and per-stage overrides; keys in localStorage; direct browser calls

steps.node: Registry with one default model and per-stage overrides; keys in localStorage; direct browser calls

items.title: Demo mode
items.summary: What the tool does when there is no key.

items.title: Local models (Ollama, LM Studio)
items.summary: They work through the OpenAI-compatible adapter with a base URL, but need CORS enabled on that server, or a desktop shell, or a proxy. Which path, and how to document it.

items.title: Mock provider with placeholder answers
items.summary: A deterministic mock answers every stage so the whole flow can be explored without a key; the UI says the answers are placeholders. Tests run on the same mock.
pros: No test ever hits the network

items.title: Block until a key is entered
items.summary: A setup screen before anything else.
cons: Nothing to see before committing a key

steps.recommended: Mock provider with placeholder answers
steps.reason: The live demo needs to work for anyone; the mock also carries the whole test suite.
steps.choose: Mock provider with placeholder answers

items.title: Two tiers, marked eagerly, checked cheaply, regenerated lazily
items.summary: Red: an ancestor selection or the root changed, so descendants are certainly stale. Yellow: a sibling decision, comment or answer changed, so possibly stale; a cheap model check on open resolves it and is remembered against the context hash. Every version records the ids it saw (root version, ancestor selections, sibling decisions, comments, answers); the hash is over ids, not text.
pros: A fresh verdict holds until the inputs change again
cons: Yellow needs a model call to clear
The rules must be exact or marks are noisy

items.title: Regenerate everything downstream on any change
items.summary: Any upstream change regenerates the subtree.

items.title: No tracking: the user re-runs what they think changed
items.summary: Nothing is marked.

steps.recommended: Two tiers, marked eagerly, checked cheaply, regenerated lazily
steps.reason: Derived views carry a hash of their inputs: a changed hash means stale, never silently wrong.
steps.choose: Two tiers, marked eagerly, checked cheaply, regenerated lazily

steps.node: Two tiers, marked eagerly, checked cheaply, regenerated lazily

items.title: Root rewrites from comments
items.summary: Comments are global amendments to the root problem. Which ones become a new root version, and what happens to the old tree.

items.title: Reusing decisions after a rewrite
items.summary: How branches under an earlier root version come back without re-deciding them.

items.title: Fold comments into a proposed rewrite the user approves; new root version, old tree red then archived
items.summary: Small comments stay as context. 'Fold into the problem' asks the model for a rewritten statement that merges them, the user approves it, the whole tree goes red and moves to 'Earlier versions'.
pros: The root stays the one source of constraints

items.title: Comments stay comments forever
items.summary: Never rewrite; the root is the original text plus a growing list.

items.title: Edit the root statement in place
items.summary: Plain editing of the statement.

steps.recommended: Fold comments into a proposed rewrite the user approves; new root version, old tree red then archived
steps.reason: A comment that changes a constraint has to reach the root, and the user must approve the wording.
steps.choose: Fold comments into a proposed rewrite the user approves; new root version, old tree red then archived

items.title: Port by hand: copy a problem with its chosen solution under the new branch, re-recorded for its new position
items.summary: 'Reuse in the current plan' copies a problem and its selection with fresh ids and freshly recorded inputs; a ported_from link keeps provenance; the copy inherits no mark.
pros: Explicit, so the user sees what carried over

items.title: Automatic merge by problem identity
items.summary: Recognise the same sub-problem and carry its decision over.
cons: Needs an identity rule (problem text plus inherited constraints) that is not designed yet

steps.recommended: Port by hand: copy a problem with its chosen solution under the new branch, re-recorded for its new position
steps.reason: Manual porting ships now; automatic merge waits for the identity rule.
steps.choose: Port by hand: copy a problem with its chosen solution under the new branch, re-recorded for its new position

items.title: Tree canvas with tidy layout, plus an outline view
items.summary: A React Flow canvas laid out by d3-hierarchy over the engine's rendered tree: the chosen path solid blue, alternatives dashed, explored-but-unchosen branches folded into a '+n explored' badge. Act on cards directly or open an inspector. An outline view shows the same brainstorm as a readable list with earlier versions.
pros: The AND-OR structure is visible at a glance
The outline keeps it readable and accessible
Layout is presentation only; every fact comes from the engine

items.title: Outline list only
items.summary: Nested rows, no canvas.
cons: Hard to see alternatives side by side

items.title: Free-form DAG canvas with manual layout
items.summary: Drag nodes anywhere.

steps.recommended: Tree canvas with tidy layout, plus an outline view
steps.reason: The outline was built first to prove the engine boundary; the canvas came last, over the same rendered tree.
steps.choose: Tree canvas with tidy layout, plus an outline view

steps.node: Tree canvas with tidy layout, plus an outline view

items.title: Small screens
items.summary: What a phone shows.

items.title: Per-node notes
items.summary: Comments are global today. Whether a node can carry its own note, and how it would feed context and staleness.

items.title: Progress and comments only, never the tree
items.summary: A phone page shows how far the brainstorm is and lets you add comments; the tree waits for a larger screen.

items.title: Zoomable canvas on phones
items.summary: The same canvas, pinch to zoom.

steps.recommended: Progress and comments only, never the tree
steps.reason: Decisions need the alternatives side by side; a phone cannot show them.
steps.choose: Progress and comments only, never the tree

steps.axis: what is generated, and from what

items.title: Several document types from the full decision tree, cached on the graph hash
items.summary: Solution design, PRD, TRD, decision records (ADR), a one-page brief, or a custom document the user describes. The model sees every decision with its rejected alternatives, pros, cons, axis, assumptions and open problems. Each document is stored with the brainstorm under a key of type, instructions and graph hash, so an unchanged brainstorm returns it instantly.
pros: Rejected options make a real TRD or ADR possible
cons: Any change to the active tree invalidates the cache

items.title: PRD only, from the decision summary
items.summary: One prompt over the code-rendered decision summary.
cons: No alternatives, so no TRD or ADR

items.title: Export the tree and write the document elsewhere
items.summary: Hand the decisions to a chat.
cons: Loses the point of deciding in the tool

steps.recommended: Several document types from the full decision tree, cached on the graph hash
steps.reason: The user asked for a document at the end which can be a PRD, TRD, solution document or something else.
steps.choose: Several document types from the full decision tree, cached on the graph hash

steps.node: Several document types from the full decision tree, cached on the graph hash

items.title: Documents across several brainstorms
items.summary: Brainstorms that belong together need one high-level structure and documents written across all of them.

items.title: A project is a lens over brainstorms, never a container
items.summary: A project stores an ordered list of brainstorm ids, a description of how they relate, and its own documents. Brainstorms never read from a project: nothing in a brainstorm's log refers to one, its context and staleness are unchanged, and one brainstorm can sit in several projects. The high-level structure is rendered by code from each brainstorm's decisions and open items; an overview document is written by the model on request.
pros: A brainstorm never changes because of a project
The overview is free and always current
cons: Connections between brainstorms are only a cheap signal: the same solution chosen twice

items.title: Shared project notes pushed into every brainstorm, with staleness marks
items.summary: A first version did this and was dropped before shipping because it made projects steer brainstorms.
cons: Marks everywhere on every note edit

items.title: One giant brainstorm instead
items.summary: Keep everything in one tree.
cons: A brainstorm cannot be reused in two contexts

steps.recommended: A project is a lens over brainstorms, never a container
steps.reason: Projects only combine brainstorms into holistic documents or a high-level structure; they never change one.
steps.choose: A project is a lens over brainstorms, never a container

steps.node: A project is a lens over brainstorms, never a container

items.title: Project storage
items.summary: A record or an event log.

items.title: Project document caching
items.summary: When a project document can be returned without a new model call.

items.title: A validated record, not an event log
items.summary: Small, user-edited metadata with no derived state worth replaying; validated with Zod on every save.

items.title: An event log like brainstorms
items.summary: Reuse the event machinery.

steps.recommended: A validated record, not an event log
steps.reason: Brainstorm logs remain the only event-sourced data.
steps.choose: A validated record, not an event log

items.title: Key on the description plus every brainstorm's graph hash in order, with doc type and instructions
items.summary: Reordering brainstorms or editing any of them produces a new document; an untouched project returns the cached one.
cons: Any edit anywhere means a new document

items.title: Never cache project documents
items.summary: Generate on every request.
cons: Pays for the same document twice

steps.recommended: Key on the description plus every brainstorm's graph hash in order, with doc type and instructions
steps.reason: Same rule as brainstorm documents, extended over every member.
steps.choose: Key on the description plus every brainstorm's graph hash in order, with doc type and instructions

steps.node: Document per graph + append-only event log

items.title: Export and import
items.summary: How a brainstorm leaves this browser and comes back.

items.title: Sync between devices and sharing
items.summary: Today everything is stored in one browser. Whether and how a brainstorm follows the user, without a backend.

items.title: Download the full event log as JSON; import replays it as a new brainstorm
items.summary: Export writes the whole log; import validates every event, replays it, and gives it a fresh id, so the same file can be imported twice without clashing.
pros: Exact history, including earlier root versions

items.title: Export the snapshot only
items.summary: Just the current document.

steps.recommended: Download the full event log as JSON; import replays it as a new brainstorm
steps.reason: The log is the source of truth; everything else is a cache.
steps.choose: Download the full event log as JSON; import replays it as a new brainstorm

steps.node: Full context with a hard ceiling, condensed past the soft ceiling

steps.instructions: Brainstorm Engine Spec: the handover document for the engine package (event log, reducer, selectors, context compiler, expansion contract, providers, staleness, documents, milestones).
Brainstorm Web Client Spec: the handover document for the web client (stack, state flow, screens, node rendering rules, persistence, provider keys and settings, milestones).
